title: MDX or rich-text JSON — the call you can't undo
description:
Most "MDX vs rich text" posts frame it as a formatting choice. It's actually a security boundary, and almost nobody mentions the CVE.

Store MDX when developers write the content and it needs React components inline. Store rich text when non-technical editors own the page and need a WYSIWYG toolbar. That's the whole decision — both handle headings, bold, links, and images fine, so the real difference is what sits in the database column: MDX is one plain string that compiles to a JavaScript component, rich text is a nested JSON tree of typed nodes that never gets compiled at all.

The portability question runs backwards from what most guides assume. MDX pulled out of a CMS is still a plain string — move it anywhere and the prose survives, only the JSX component tags need re-registering. A rich text tree is portable in theory and painful in practice: Contentful's tree shape and Sanity's tree shape are different, so moving between them means writing a serializer per node type, plus another for every embedded reference. That's a converter project, not a git mv.

Here's the part that gets skipped: MDX from a CMS is remote code, not inert data. Rich text JSON just gets walked and rendered — nothing executes. MDX compiles, and if any editor can submit MDX that your server compiles, you're running content-authored code server-side. This already happened: next-mdx-remote versions 4.3.0 through 5.0.0 allowed arbitrary code execution during React server-side rendering of untrusted MDX (CVE-2026-0969, disclosed February 2026). Version 6.0.0 fixed it by blocking JavaScript expressions by default. The rule that follows is short — trusted authors, MDX is fine; untrusted or public submissions, block expressions or store rich text instead.

Rich text still wins outright for three real cases: non-technical editors who want a toolbar and a compile error is a support ticket; multi-channel output, since one JSON tree serializes to HTML, PDF, mobile, or plain text where MDX assumes a JSX runtime on the other end; and real-time co-editing, which needs a structured tree underneath to merge live edits at all.

The option most comparisons skip entirely: keep structure out of the prose. Author, date, tags, hero image — none of that belongs in a content blob, it belongs in typed fields you can query and validate. The prose field then only holds prose, and the format question gets a lot smaller.

Full breakdown — the comparison table, the component-allowlist security model, and what actually breaks in production for each format: https://draftbase.co/mdx-editor/vs/mdx-vs-rich-text

More on this in r/draftbase_cms: https://reddit.com/r/draftbase_cms

Draftbase templates hold typed fields for structure and a richText field that stores plain MDX beside them. Hobby is free, Startup is $49/mo.

title: Building a Custom Map Drawing Toolbar in React Without Coupling UI to the Map
description:
How to separate drawing state, application controls, and map rendering so your UI can evolve independently of the map engine.

Map drawing looks simple until it becomes part of a real application.

A user clicks a polygon tool, draws a boundary, and saves it. Then the product requirements grow: the toolbar needs to live in a sidebar, the selected shape needs an editable name, colors need to come from the application’s design system, undo and redo need to work from keyboard shortcuts, and annotations need to persist alongside the rest of the project data.

At that point, drawing is no longer just a map control. It is application state.

This article explores how to structure a React drawing experience so the map handles geographic interaction and rendering, while the application owns the workflow. We’ll build a custom toolbar using react-map-annotate, an open-source library I created to make that separation practical across multiple map engines.

The coupling problem

Many drawing integrations begin with an imperative API:

const draw = new MapDrawingControl();

map.addControl(draw);

// Later, somewhere in the application:
draw.changeMode("draw_polygon");

This is a perfectly reasonable model for a self-contained map tool. The difficulty appears when the rest of the application needs to participate.

You may end up maintaining several representations of the same state:

Application toolbar
       ↓
Drawing control mode
       ↓
Drawing control feature store
       ↓
Map events
       ↓
React state
       ↓
Application sidebar / database

Now consider a user renaming a polygon in the sidebar. The application updates its state, but the drawing control may still have its own feature representation. You need to synchronize the change back. Selection, deletion, styling, and undo history can introduce similar coordination problems.

The issue is not that imperative drawing APIs are inherently bad. It is that the drawing control has become the owner of state that the application also needs to own.

For a React application with a custom design system, I prefer a different boundary:

Application state
       ↓
Drawing session
       ├── Custom toolbar
       ├── Annotation sidebar
       ├── Keyboard shortcuts
       ├── Persistence
       └── Map adapter
              ↓
           Map engine

The map is still responsible for pointer interaction, coordinate projection, and rendering. But it is no longer the center of the application’s drawing workflow.

The architecture: session, UI, and adapter

The approach used by react-map-annotate separates drawing into three responsibilities.

1. The drawing session

The session owns concepts such as the active tool, draft geometry, selection, annotation changes, and drawing actions.

Your application can access those actions through React hooks instead of reaching into a map instance.

2. The application UI

The toolbar, annotation list, property inspector, and keyboard shortcuts are consumers of the session. They do not need to know whether the map underneath is Mapbox or Leaflet.

This means the same drawing action can be triggered from a toolbar button, a command palette, or a keyboard shortcut.

3. The map adapter

The adapter translates the session into map-specific rendering and interaction. Each engine has different APIs for layers, markers, projection, and pointer events, but those details stay behind the adapter boundary.

The library currently provides adapters for Mapbox, MapLibre, Google Maps, Leaflet, and ArcGIS, with a shared annotation model.

Building a custom toolbar

Let’s start with a Mapbox example. The important part is that the toolbar is not a child of the map. It is a sibling that consumes the same provider.

Install the package and the Mapbox dependencies:

npm install @orange-groove/react-map-annotate react-map-gl mapbox-gl

Now create a small drawing application:

import { useState } from "react";
import Map from "react-map-gl/mapbox";

import {
  AnnotateProvider,
  useAnnotateTools,
  type Annotation,
} from "@orange-groove/react-map-annotate/core";

import { Annotate } from "@orange-groove/react-map-annotate/mapbox";

import "@orange-groove/react-map-annotate/styles.css";

function DrawingToolbar() {
  const {
    items,
    finish,
    canFinish,
    undo,
    redo,
    canUndo,
    canRedo,
    selectedId,
    deleteSelected,
  } = useAnnotateTools();

  return (
    <div role="toolbar" aria-label="Map drawing tools">
      {items.map((item) => (
        <button
          key={item.id}
          type="button"
          aria-pressed={item.active}
          onClick={item.select}
        >
          {item.label}
        </button>
      ))}

      <button type="button" disabled={!canFinish} onClick={finish}>
        Finish
      </button>

      <button type="button" disabled={!canUndo} onClick={undo}>
        Undo
      </button>

      <button type="button" disabled={!canRedo} onClick={redo}>
        Redo
      </button>

      <button
        type="button"
        disabled={!selectedId}
        onClick={deleteSelected}
      >
        Delete
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

export function DrawingApp({ token }: { token: string }) {
  const [annotations, setAnnotations] = useState<Annotation[]>([]);

  return (
    <AnnotateProvider
      annotations={annotations}
      onChange={setAnnotations}
    >
      <div className="drawing-layout">
        <aside className="drawing-sidebar">
          <DrawingToolbar />
        </aside>

        <main className="map-container">
          <Map
            mapboxAccessToken={token}
            initialViewState={{
              longitude: -81.1,
              latitude: 32.0,
              zoom: 12,
            }}
            mapStyle="mapbox://styles/mapbox/streets-v12"
            style={{ width: "100%", height: "100%" }}
          >
            <Annotate />
          </Map>
        </main>
      </div>
    </AnnotateProvider>
  );
}

The toolbar does not receive a mapRef. It does not call map.addControl(). It does not need to know how Mapbox represents drawing modes.

It receives a list of available tools and actions from the drawing session. The map adapter consumes that same session and renders the interaction.

The bundled toolbar is optional; the application can replace it entirely.

Controlling drawing from anywhere

Sometimes a generic toolbar is not enough. You may have a command palette, a workflow-specific button, or a form that needs to start a particular drawing action.

The lower-level useAnnotate() hook exposes the session directly:

import { useAnnotate } from
  "@orange-groove/react-map-annotate/core";

function BoundaryActions() {
  const {
    tool,
    setTool,
    finish,
    canFinish,
  } = useAnnotate();

  return (
    <section>
      <button
        type="button"
        aria-pressed={tool === "polygon"}
        onClick={() => setTool("polygon")}
      >
        Draw boundary
      </button>

      <button
        type="button"
        disabled={!canFinish}
        onClick={finish}
      >
        Save boundary shape
      </button>
    </section>
  );
}

This is useful when drawing is part of a larger workflow. For example, a site-planning application might have a “Define property boundary” step. The user does not need to interact with a generic drawing toolbar at all; the workflow can activate the polygon tool directly.

The same principle applies to keyboard shortcuts, contextual menus, and custom controls built with Chakra UI, MUI, Radix, or your own component system.

Editing annotations from a sidebar

Drawing the geometry is only the first part of most applications. Users also need to name, style, select, and delete their annotations.

The library exposes those operations through useAnnotateItems():

import { useAnnotateItems } from
  "@orange-groove/react-map-annotate/core";

function AnnotationSidebar() {
  const items = useAnnotateItems();

  return (
    <aside>
      <h2>Annotations</h2>

      {items.map((item) => (
        <div key={item.id}>
          <button
            type="button"
            aria-pressed={item.isSelected}
            onClick={item.select}
          >
            {item.annotation.label || "Untitled annotation"}
          </button>

          <input
            aria-label="Annotation name"
            value={item.annotation.label ?? ""}
            onChange={(event) =>
              item.setLabel(event.target.value)
            }
          />

          <input
            type="color"
            aria-label="Annotation color"
            value={item.annotation.color ?? "#2563eb"}
            onChange={(event) =>
              item.setColor(event.target.value)
            }
          />

          <button type="button" onClick={item.remove}>
            Delete
          </button>
        </div>
      ))}
    </aside>
  );
}

The sidebar is not scraping information from a map overlay. It is operating on the annotation session directly.

That distinction matters when you add more application behavior. A property inspector can update stroke width. A project form can rename an annotation. A bulk action can delete selected items. The map does not need to become the API through which every application feature passes.

Keeping persistence at the application boundary

The provider can receive controlled annotations and an onChange callback:

const [annotations, setAnnotations] = useState<Annotation[]>([]);

<AnnotateProvider
  annotations={annotations}
  onChange={setAnnotations}
>
  {/* Map and application UI */}
</AnnotateProvider>

This makes persistence an application concern.

For example, you might debounce changes before saving them to an API:

function useSaveAnnotations(
  projectId: string,
  annotations: Annotation[]
) {
  // Your application can debounce, validate, and persist
  // the annotation array using its existing data layer.
}

Or you could store the annotations in Zustand, Redux, or another state-management solution.

The important architectural point is that persistence does not need to ask the map for its current features. The application already has the data it intends to save.

In a production system, I would also keep server-side validation, authorization, and any required coordinate-system transformations in the persistence layer. A drawing library should not be responsible for deciding who is allowed to modify a project.

Avoiding map-engine lock-in

A common concern with map-heavy applications is that the rendering engine may change. Pricing, licensing, performance, or product requirements can make a migration necessary.

If your drawing UI is tightly coupled to one engine’s control API, migration becomes more than replacing the map component. You may also need to rewrite the toolbar, selection behavior, feature synchronization, and persistence logic.

With an adapter-based architecture, the application-facing session can remain stable while the map integration changes.

For example, the Mapbox adapter is imported from:

import { Annotate } from
  "@orange-groove/react-map-annotate/mapbox";

The MapLibre adapter uses:

import { Annotate } from
  "@orange-groove/react-map-annotate/maplibre";

The surrounding provider, custom toolbar, annotation list, and application state can continue using the core API.

This does not mean every map engine has identical capabilities. Terrain, markers, rendering, and engine-specific behavior still require adapter-specific handling. The goal is to isolate those differences rather than spread them throughout the application.

What belongs in the drawing library?

A useful boundary is to ask whether a feature is part of drawing interaction or part of the application’s business workflow.

The drawing library should handle things such as geometry creation, editing handles, selection, draft state, and rendering. The application should own project permissions, database persistence, business-specific validation, and the surrounding user experience.

For example, a field-service application might require a polygon to be named before it can be saved. That validation belongs in the application. The drawing session should expose the geometry and actions needed to implement it.

This separation also makes the library easier to reuse. A real-estate application, a GIS dashboard, and a site-planning tool can share drawing behavior without sharing the same toolbar or business rules.

Tradeoffs and alternatives

There are good reasons to use an existing map-native drawing control. If you need a simple polygon tool with a standard toolbar, a library such as Mapbox GL Draw, Leaflet.Draw, or Terra Draw may be a better fit.

Terra Draw in particular provides an adapter-based approach and programmatic drawing modes. It is a capable option for developers who want to assemble drawing behavior around different map engines.

The approach described here is aimed at a different integration preference: a React session that exposes drawing state and actions to the rest of the component tree, with optional stock UI and a shared annotation model.

That comes with its own tradeoffs. A headless API gives you more control, but it also means you are responsible for designing the user experience. You need to think about disabled states, accessibility, keyboard behavior, persistence, and how drawing fits into the rest of your application.

For complex products, that control is often exactly what you need.

Try it in your own application

react-map-annotate is MIT licensed and available on npm. It includes drawing and editing tools for polygons, rectangles, circles, lines, arrows, freehand paths, markers, text, and measurements, along with optional toolbar and annotation-list components.

The repository includes examples for custom toolbars, custom lists, headless usage, and the supported map engines.

  • GitHub: https://github.com/orange-groove/react-map-annotate
  • npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@orange-groove/react-map-annotate

I’m especially interested in feedback from developers building GIS dashboards, field-service applications, site-planning tools, or other map-heavy React products. If you have had to work around a drawing control to integrate it with your application’s state or design system, I’d like to hear what the difficult parts were.

The broader idea is simple: drawing should be a capability of your application, not an isolated control that your application has to work around.

title: GitHub - orange-groove/react-map-annotate: Draw on Mapbox, MapLibre, Google, Leaflet, or ArcGIS in React
description:
I built an open-source React map drawing library because I got tired of fighting drawing controls that wanted to own the UI.

react-map-annotate lets your application control the drawing session. Put the toolbar in your sidebar, header, or command palette. Select tools, finish shapes, edit labels and colors, undo/redo, and persist annotations through React state.

It supports Mapbox, MapLibre, Google Maps, Leaflet, and ArcGIS through separate adapters, with a shared annotation model.

The goal is simple: the map should render the drawing, not dictate how your application works.

It includes freehand drawing, polygons, rectangles, circles, arrows, markers, text, and measurement tools, along with editing handles and a headless API.

The project is MIT licensed and available on npm. I’d love feedback from developers building GIS, field-service, site-planning, or other map-heavy applications—especially anyone who has had to work around existing drawing controls.

GitHub: https://github.com/orange-groove/react-map-annotate

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@orange-groove/react-map-annotate

What would you need from a drawing library before using it in a production application?

title: Silent HMAC Key Contamination: Uncovering a Logic Flaw in Burp's JWT Editor Extension
description:
How a failing Web Security Academy lab led to a root-cause analysis of a hidden bug

JWT Editor was shortlisted for "Best Auth & Access Control" in PortSwigger's 2026 Burp Suite Extension Awards. This is the story of finding a silent bug inside it.

Usually, when something goes wrong, your first instinct is to look at yourself. What did I do wrong? Which step did I miss? It takes a lot to get to the point where you seriously consider that the mistake isn't yours at all: it's the tool's.

It's a bit like a developer insisting their code is broken because of VS Code itself. Especially when everyone around you is saying the opposite, and your own eyes keep telling you the same thing they're saying. But sometimes you have to hold onto an old piece of advice:

"Once you eliminate the impossible, whatever remains, no matter how improbable, must be the truth."
— Arthur Conan Doyle (Sherlock Holmes)

This is the story of how a training lab that "shouldn't have been failing" turned into a fifteen-hour investigation, a silent bug, and a GitHub issue against the #1 most popular extension in the Burp Suite BApp Store as of today.

Some Background: What Is JWT Algorithm Confusion?

Before the story makes sense, you need the theory behind it. JWT algorithm confusion is a class of vulnerability that stems from how some backend libraries implement token verification. Some implementations write code like this:

publicKey = <public-key-of-server>;
token = request.getCookie("session");
verify(token, publicKey);

The problem is that if the server receives a token signed with a symmetric algorithm like HS256 instead of the expected asymmetric RS256, some libraries' generic verify() method will happily treat the public key (which is, by definition, public and known to anyone) as if it were an HMAC secret. If an attacker can get their hands on that public key, they can sign their own token with it using HS256, and the server will trust it.

If you want the full technical breakdown, PortSwigger's own write-up on algorithm confusion covers it properly. I'm only summarizing it here because it's the whole reason I ended up down this rabbit hole in the first place.

The Lab, and the First 50 Minutes of Denial

Once I'd finished the theory, I moved to the practical lab: JWT authentication bypass via algorithm confusion.

The intended solution is straightforward: grab the exposed public key from the lab's /jwks.json endpoint, convert it to PEM, Base64-encode it, use that as the HMAC secret, switch the header's alg from RS256 to HS256, change the payload's sub from wiener to administrator, sign the forged token, log in, and delete carlos's account. Lab solved.

Except it wasn't. I followed every step exactly, right up to sending the forged token, and it was never accepted. No administrator access, no matter how many times I repeated it. After about 50 minutes on my own, I assumed I was missing something before that final signing step, so I opened the official walkthrough. It was exactly what I'd already done, word for word. So I told myself: maybe I'm misreading the intent of a step, even if the words are right.

So I went looking at community solution videos. Here's where it got strange: three or four different people, same steps, same order, no hidden tricks. Comments underneath were full of people thanking them, confirming it worked. So why wasn't it working for me?

At that point I could've closed the lab, marked it "watched the solution," and moved on. But that never sits right with me. "It happens because it happens" has never been a satisfying explanation for me. If something isn't working, there's a reason, you just haven't found it yet.

Ruling Out the Obvious: Isolating Variables

So I decided to take a more disciplined approach: isolate every variable, one at a time, instead of assuming.

First variable: is this lab instance broken?

I closed the lab and waited about 15 minutes for it to disconnect. If you've used PortSwigger's Academy labs before, you know they're not static; the internal state (including the public key at /jwks.json) regenerates on a fresh instance, and even credentials you've already used will stop working after a while, requiring you to redo the earlier steps to get back to where you were.

After a short break and a cup of black coffee, I opened a brand-new instance and repeated everything carefully. Still failed. Okay, that rules out "this specific lab instance is glitched." The problem wasn't the lab.

Second variable: is the exposed public key itself wrong?

Maybe, I thought, PortSwigger had recently changed something about how the lab exposes its key at /jwks.json, and the "official" approach was simply outdated. So I decided to solve the lab a completely different way, using an independent tool: rsa_sign2n (a simplified fork of jwt_forgery.py), run via Docker:

docker run --rm -it portswigger/sig2n <token1> <token2>

This tool takes two JWTs signed with the same RSA key and derives the key material from them, outputting:

  • A Base64-encoded PEM key, in both X.509 and PKCS1 format.
  • A forged JWT signed with each of these derived keys.

Since I knew this lab used an X.509-format key, I copied the public key with that format, and went into JWT Editor. I created a New Symmetric Key, pasted the value into the k parameter, saved it, changed wiener to administrator, switched the header's alg to HS256, signed the token, and sent the request.

It worked. No unauthorized response. The forged token was accepted. carlos deleted. Lab solved.

The Comparison That Changed Everything

Now I had something concrete: a public key that worked (from rsa_sign2n) and a public key that didn't (from following the official steps). I re-ran the original method again just to be sure, and, as expected, it failed again.

Looking at both Base64-encoded strings side by side, there was a visible difference between them. My first assumption was that the lab's /jwks.json endpoint was serving a genuinely broken key. But when I Base64-decoded both of them back into PEM format:

-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----
MIIBIjANBgkqhkiG9w0BAQEFAAOCAQ8AMIIBCgKCAQEA..

They were identical. Same characters, same order, no difference at all. My first theory was wrong. But there was still clearly something different between the two of them: something invisible in Burp's UI, something the human eye wasn't catching.

With a slight smile forming, I opened Burp Comparer, pasted both PEM versions in (before any Base64 encoding), and switched to Hex view. About four hours in, the difference finally showed itself, plain and unmistakable.

Video Source

One of the two was full of extra bytes 0D. Going back to the Decoder's Hex view, I could see that 0D appeared exactly once, at the end of every single line.

Note: 0D is the hex value for a Carriage Return (\r), while 0A is the hex value for a Line Feed (\n).

A Quick Detour: Why Do Line Endings Even Differ Between Operating Systems?

This goes back to mechanical teletypewriters, decades before any of the operating systems we use today existed. A teletypewriter needed two separate physical actions to start a new line: a Carriage Return (CR) to send the print head back to the start of the line, and a Line Feed (LF) to advance the paper by one line. Early computer systems inherited this literally, sending both characters, \r\n, to represent a new line.

When Unix was designed, Ken Thompson made a deliberate simplification: use \n alone as the line terminator, since a single character was enough on a screen (no physical print head to return). Classic Mac OS, on the other hand, went the opposite way and used \r alone. Microsoft's MS-DOS, and later Windows, kept the original \r\n pair for compatibility with older systems and printers, and that convention has stuck around ever since, all the way to the Windows 11 I was using in 2026.

Modern macOS, being Unix-based since OS X, switched to \n like Linux. So today, in practice, it comes down to: Windows uses \r\n; Linux and macOS use \n.

It's a little funny, honestly: a bug appearing in 2026 because of a decision made decades ago, for a piece of hardware that stopped existing before most of us were born.

Reverse-Engineering Backwards

After the discovery, I felt considerably calmer. I finished my coffee, stepped outside for some air for about half an hour (four hours of near-continuous sitting had left my body stiff) and came back with a clear head.

I went back into the lab, but this time as a different person: I knew what the problem was; now I just needed to reverse-engineer where exactly it was being introduced, all the way back to the point where I pasted the public key into Burp Decoder, before any Base64 encoding.

Step one: copy the key directly from /jwks.json and paste it into Decoder's Hex view. Result: no extra bytes.

Step two: convert that same key to PEM using JWT Editor, then paste that into Decoder's Hex view. Result: the bytes appear.

The culprit was JWT Editor. But did the corruption happen during copying, or during pasting? The surprising answer was: neither. It happens before any copy-paste at all. Going back into JWT Editor and generating a brand-new, random RSA key, then converting it to PEM, the bytes were already there, automatically. I confirmed this in the simplest way possible: placing the cursor at the end of any line and pressing Backspace. The visible character wasn't deleted on the first press; it took a second press. That first, invisible deletion was the hidden \r.

To confirm that none of the available copy methods were stripping the \r, I tested every one of them: Ctrl+C, right-click copy, and the extension's own "Copy Public Key as PEM" button. Every single one produced the exact same result once pasted into Decoder: the extra 0D bytes were always there.

Video Source

Into the Source Code

I went to the extension's page on the BApp Store, found its link to PortSwigger's Github repository, and traced it to the maintainer's repository.

Eventually, I landed on the exact file responsible: PEMUtils.java.

The relevant method:

public static String pemObjectToString(PemObject pemObject) throws IOException {
    StringWriter stringWriter = new StringWriter();
    PemWriter pemWriter = new PemWriter(stringWriter);
    pemWriter.writeObject(pemObject);
    pemWriter.close();
    stringWriter.close();
    return stringWriter.toString();
}

PemWriter comes from BouncyCastle (org.bouncycastle.util.io.pem.PemWriter), and it directly extends java.io.BufferedWriter. It doesn't define its own line-break logic: when writeObject() inserts line breaks (every 64 Base64 characters, per RFC 1421, plus around the header/footer), it relies on the inherited BufferedWriter.newLine() method. Per the JDK documentation, that method "writes a line separator... defined by the system property line.separator," which defaults to \r\n on Windows. Since pemObjectToString() returns the raw string with no normalization step, whatever the host OS's line separator is gets baked directly into every PEM string the tool produces.

  • Setup note: the exact environment I was running when I found this was: Windows 11 Pro, Version 25H2 (OS Build 26200.8875), Burp Suite Community Edition v2026.7.2, JWT Editor version 2.6.1 (updated 23 Apr 2026). I'm noting this specifically because both Burp and its extensions update regularly; this reflects the state of things at the time the bug was found, not necessarily whatever version you're reading this on.

The fix itself is small and low-risk:

public static String pemObjectToString(PemObject pemObject) throws IOException {
    StringWriter stringWriter = new StringWriter();
    PemWriter pemWriter = new PemWriter(stringWriter);
    pemWriter.writeObject(pemObject);
    pemWriter.close();
    stringWriter.close();

    // Normalize line endings for consistent cross-platform output
    return stringWriter.toString().replace("\r\n", "\n");
}

Worth noting: this line is completely safe on every platform. .replace() only acts when it finds a match. On Linux and macOS, where the output is already \n-only, there's nothing to replace; the string comes back untouched.

Why This Went Unnoticed

Most people working in web security and bug bounty hunting use Linux or macOS, not native Windows, whether that’s a pentesting distro, WSL, or a Mac. On both, this bug simply doesn’t exist, since their line separator is already \n. The solution videos I watched, where the authors were using JWT Editor extension, and the comments thanking them for a walkthrough that "just worked," almost certainly all originated from Linux or macOS. Even if someone failed to solve this on Windows, they would probably assume it was just a lab error or a mistake on their end. If they did realize it was a bug, they wouldn't spend hours trying to figure it out in a simple lab, especially with such a silent issue, so they would probably just move on.

A Manual Workaround Exists, But...

There is a trivial workaround: pasting the exported PEM into an external text editor and copying it back out strips the \r, since most standard text applications don't preserve it on that round trip. But there's no logical reason to bounce your key through an external editor unless you already suspect the bug exists.

Reporting It

Once I had a confirmed root cause, a working fix, and a reproducible demonstration, I put together a full report and opened issue #248 directly on the maintainer's repository.

From the very first attempt at the lab to submitting that issue, the whole thing took roughly ten hours of actual focused work, not counting the short breaks in between.

Testing the Fix Myself

While waiting for a response from the maintainer, I decided not to just leave the fix as theory. On August 07, 2026, I loaded the original extension’s JAR file into Recaf, a tool for editing compiled Java bytecode directly, and applied the exact one-line fix from the report directly to the compiled class.

With the patch in place, I exported the JAR as a separate test build (renamed to "JWT Editor (Test Build)" to avoid any confusion with the original) and loaded it into Burp as a new extension. It worked: generating a fresh RSA key and converting it to PEM no longer produced the extra 0D bytes, and the rest of the extension's functionality behaved exactly as expected.

Video Source

And once I confirmed the fix worked, I opened pull request #249 against the maintainer's repository with the same one-line change, so it could be reviewed and merged into the official codebase.

Furthermore, I tested this patched build on Kali Linux, confirming that the LF normalization works flawlessly across environments and will absolutely not break the extension for macOS or Linux users.

Between bytecode editing in Recaf, testing the build, and putting together the pull request, it took me an additional five hours.

First Response and Discussion With the Maintainer

On August 21, 2026, I got the first response from the maintainer, and after a long and detailed discussion, here's where things stand:

  • A) The official lab solution is still broken for Windows users if followed exactly as written. The maintainer declined to merge my pull request #249, and I now agree with his reasoning (details below).
  • B) The HMAC Key Confusion attack feature in the tool has since been improved and now handles this scenario correctly, including for Windows users. This gives a more reliable path through the lab (also below).

The maintainer and I ultimately agreed this isn't really a bug in the extension itself: "Copy as PEM" is meant as a general export feature, so platform-specific line endings make sense there. It wasn't designed for a workflow that treats the exported text as raw secret bytes, which is what this attack does. That's why the PR was declined.

There's also a more practical reason my fix wasn't the ideal solution, even setting the "design intent" argument aside: it normalized every PEM output to Linux-style (\n) line endings. That works for this specific lab, since Linux-hosted backends are the common case, and it does solve it. But it's not the most robust fix, because if the backend server happened to be Windows-based instead, the exact same key-confusion mismatch could resurface in the opposite direction: the PEM export would be \n-only while the server's stored key material used \r\n. Hardcoding one platform's convention solves the common case, but doesn't fully generalize to every backend.

The Better, Updated Way to Solve the Lab and Perform the Attack

The maintainer has since built proper support for this scenario directly into the HMAC Key Confusion attack feature, released in version 2.6.2 on September 04, 2026.

The updated, more reliable workflow is:

  1. 1. Visit the /jwks.json endpoint and copy the JSON
  2. In JWT Editor, click "Import JWK Set" (bottom right).
  3. Paste the JSON and click Import.
  4. Get a valid JWT in Repeater, then edit the sub field.
  5. Click Attack, then select "HMAC Key Confusion."
  6. Pick the key you just imported.
  7. Choose one of the four line-ending options depending on the backend server's platform and how it stores its PEM key:
    • Linux/macOS (0x0A)
    • Linux/macOS (0x0A) – no trailing newline
    • Windows (0x0D0A)
    • Windows (0x0D0A) – no trailing newline

(Most real-world backends are Linux-hosted, as in the PortSwigger lab, so the first option is usually the right starting point. That said, even on a Linux backend it's worth trying the other Linux/macOS option too if the first one doesn't work, since not every server handles the PEM key identically.)

  1. Click OK. The forged token now has a valid signature.

Important note: if you can't find the "Import JWK Set" button in the bottom right, make sure the Scaling option is enabled in Burp Suite, and keep Burp's display font size under 18.

This matters because using too large a font size, or a Windows display scale setting above 100% (under Windows display settings), causes the "Import JWK Set" button to get cut off in Burp Suite's UI, as shown below.

One last thing worth mentioning: when I first started chasing this, I was only 83 days into cybersecurity. And it only happened because "it happens because it happens" never satisfies me.

Reaching Out to PortSwigger

I didn't mention this earlier in the writeup, but as soon as I ran into the bug, I sent an email to PortSwigger at support@portswigger.net. They responded and pointed me to the maintainer's repository, where I had already opened Issue #248 the day before. But even after everything was resolved, the bug still exists in the lab's official solution and in the theoretical explanation on PortSwigger's site for Windows users, so I followed up with a second email. Here's their reply:

If they make any changes on their end, whether in the theoretical write-up, the lab's official solution, or in a follow-up email to me, I'll update this write-up accordingly.

Timeline

  • Aug 03, 2026: Sent an initial email to PortSwigger about the bug.
  • Aug 03, 2026: Root cause identified after isolating variables in the lab.
  • Aug 03, 2026: Submitted GitHub Issue #248 to the maintainer's repository with a detailed PoC.
  • Aug 04, 2026: PortSwigger replied, pointing me toward the maintainer's repository, where I had already opened Issue #248 the day before.
  • Aug 07, 2026: Patched the bytecode locally via Recaf to verify the fix on a custom test build.
  • Aug 07, 2026: Submitted pull request #249 containing the cross-platform line-ending normalization fix.
  • Aug 21, 2026: Received the first response from the maintainer.
  • Aug 21 – Sep 01, 2026: Discussion with the maintainer.
  • Sep 04, 2026: JWT Editor 2.6.2 released.
  • Sep 04, 2026: Sent a follow-up email to PortSwigger after the extension update, noting the lab solution and docs still weren't updated.
  • Sep 07, 2026: Received PortSwigger's reply to the follow-up email.

"Silent bugs don't raise flags; you have to look under the hood."

title: Why You Need a Real Download Manager in 2026 (And Why I Switched to NeXDM)
description:
If you're still downloading files straight through Chrome or Edge in 2026, you're leaving a huge chunk of your internet connection on the table. This post breaks down why browser downloads are no longer good enough, what's wrong with the "classic" download managers everyone already knows, and why I ended up settling on NeXDM as my daily driver.

The Problem: Your Browser Wasn't Built for 2026-Sized Files

A few things have changed that make a plain browser download feel increasingly broken:

  1. Files got huge

50–100GB game installs, 4K/8K video archives, and multi-gigabyte AI model checkpoints are now completely normal downloads — not edge cases.

  1. Your fast internet is being wasted

Most browsers still pull a file over a single TCP connection. It doesn't matter if you're paying for 300 Mbps or a full 1 Gbps fiber line — a single-stream download typically caps out around 20–25 MB/s, because one connection can only push so much data at once. The rest of your bandwidth just... sits there unused.

  1. One bad Wi-Fi blip = start over

Download a 30GB file in-browser, have your connection drop for two seconds at 95% complete, and there's a good chance the whole thing fails or restarts from scratch. Painful, and it happens more often than it should.

  1. Servers throttle single connections

Services like Google Drive, Mega, or generic file hosts often cap the speed of a single connection per user — which is exactly what your browser is using.

Why the "Usual" Download Managers Don't Cut It Either

If you've looked into this before, you've probably run into the same handful of names — and the same handful of complaints:

Tool The Catch
IDM (Internet Download Manager) 30-day trial, then a paid license (~$24). This pushes a lot of people toward cracked/patched versions floating around the internet — which is its own security risk. UI still looks like it's from the Windows XP era.
JDownloader 2 Built on Java, which means real overhead — 350MB+ RAM just sitting in the background — plus installers that try to bundle extra offers if you're not careful.
Free Download Manager (FDM) A 100MB+ install and ~150MB of RAM usage while it's just running, which noticeably drags on lower-end machines.
uTorrent / BitTorrent clients Historically loaded with ads, pop-ups, and bundled software during setup.

Basically: you either pay, deal with bloat, or deal with ads. None of those are great defaults for something that should just quietly move bytes for you.

Enter NeXDM

NeXDM is a free, open-architecture Windows download manager built natively in Rust, designed around one core idea: split a download into many parallel segments so you actually use the bandwidth you're paying for.

The core engine: 64-segment parallel downloading

Where most managers cap out at 8 (or sometimes 32) simultaneous connections per file, NeXDM splits a single download into 64 parallel segments. Instead of pulling data through one narrow pipe, it opens many at once — which is how it gets past the per-connection throttling that services like Drive or Mega apply, and why it can push much closer to your actual line speed.

On NeXDM's own published gigabit benchmarks, that's the difference between a browser's single-stream ~25.4 MB/s and NeXDM's ~248.6 MB/s on the same connection — a roughly 10x jump. (You can check their methodology and raw benchmark data yourself on the benchmarks page.) In real terms, their site shows a 10GB game-asset download going from about 6:40 minutes down to roughly 42 seconds.

Genuinely lightweight — because it's written in Rust

This is the part that surprised me most. NeXDM ships as a ~5MB installer, and because it's built in Rust instead of something like Java or Electron, it idles at a tiny memory footprint instead of the 150–350MB+ some competitors use just sitting in the background. Translation: it doesn't fight your game, your IDE, or your browser tabs for RAM while it's quietly downloading something in the background.

Two tools in one: HTTP downloads + native BitTorrent

You don't need to run a separate torrent client alongside it. NeXDM has a native BitTorrent/magnet-link engine built directly into the app (powered by the open-source librqbit engine), so both your direct downloads and your torrents live in one place — no extra install, no extra background process.

It's actually verified, not just "trust me"

A few things worth checking yourself rather than taking my word for it:

It's Microsoft Store certified (Store ID: 9NTMZ6V1GZ3V), so installing from the Store gives you a clean, warning-free install.
Every release ships with a published SHA-256 checksum you can verify against the binary, documented on their security page.
It's referenced on the Wikipedia comparison of download managers page.
Resume that actually resumes

Because the file is already tracked as 64 independent segments, if your connection drops, NeXDM resumes from exactly where each segment left off instead of restarting the whole file. No more losing a 95%-complete download to a two-second Wi-Fi hiccup.

It's actually free — not a trial

There's no license key, no credit card, and no feature paywall. The 64-segment engine, the BitTorrent core, and the browser integration are all unlocked from install. (The project accepts optional donations via Buy Me a Coffee / UPI if you want to support ongoing development, but nothing is gated behind it.)

Quick Comparison
Typical Free Downloader NeXDM
Installer size 50MB+ ~5MB
Parallel segments 8 64
Background RAM 150MB+ Minimal (near-zero)
BitTorrent built in Rarely Yes (native)
Resume reliability Inconsistent Segment-level resume
Cost Free trial → paid, or ad-supported Free, fully unlocked
Getting Started
Grab the installer from the Microsoft Store (zero SmartScreen warnings) or the direct .exe from nexdm.in/download.
Run the setup — it's a lightweight installer, done in seconds.
Install the companion browser extension (works with Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera) so NeXDM automatically catches large-file links instead of routing them through your browser's default downloader.
Drop in a magnet link or torrent file directly if you need P2P downloads — no separate client required.
Final Thoughts

None of this matters if you're just downloading the occasional 5MB PDF — your browser is fine for that. But the moment you're regularly pulling down large game installs, 4K footage, ISOs, or big model checkpoints, the gap between a single-stream browser download and a proper segmented download manager becomes very real, very fast. NeXDM's pitch — genuinely lightweight, genuinely free, and built for how big files actually are in 2026 — is why it's replaced both IDM and my old torrent client on my machine.

If you want to see the raw numbers for yourself rather than take a blog post's word for it, the benchmark methodology and checksum verification steps are both public.

title: Why You Need a Download Manager in 2026 — And What Makes NeXDM Different
description:
Why You Need a Download Manager in 2026 — And What Makes NeXDM Different

In 2026, downloading a file isn't what it used to be.

We're no longer downloading just a few megabytes.

We're downloading 50GB+ games, 4K/8K videos, Linux ISOs, AI models, datasets, VM images, software packages, and huge archives.

At the same time, internet speeds have dramatically increased.

300 Mbps.
500 Mbps.
1 Gbps.
Even faster.

So why does a large download sometimes still feel slow?

And why can a temporary network interruption turn a large download into a frustrating experience?

That's the problem a modern download manager should solve.

The Problem With Large Downloads

Let's say you're downloading a 50GB file.

Your internet connection is fast, but the download is only using a fraction of your available bandwidth.

Or perhaps you're at 95% and your connection suddenly drops.

You don't want to start over.

You want the download to resume intelligently.

This is where a dedicated download manager becomes useful.

1. Large Files Need Better Download Management

Modern files are getting bigger.

A single download can now be:

  • 🎮 50–100GB+ game
  • 🎬 4K/8K video
  • 🤖 AI model or dataset
  • 💿 Operating-system ISO
  • 🧑‍💻 Developer SDK or toolchain
  • 📦 Backup/archive
  • 🖥️ Virtual machine image

When files become this large, download reliability matters just as much as download speed.

A failed 500MB download is annoying.

A failed 80GB download is painful.

2. Why Segmented Downloading Matters

One technique used by download managers is segmented downloading.

Instead of downloading the entire file through one continuous transfer, the downloader can request different byte ranges simultaneously when the server supports HTTP range requests.

Conceptually:

Single download

SERVER ───────────────────> PC
          Entire file


Segmented download

SERVER ──┬── Segment 1 ───> PC
         ├── Segment 2 ───> PC
         ├── Segment 3 ───> PC
         ├── ...
         └── Segment N ───> PC

This can help utilize available bandwidth more effectively under the right server and network conditions.

NeXDM takes this approach with support for up to 64 parallel download segments.

However, there's an important point:

More connections don't automatically mean more speed.

Actual performance depends on the server, network conditions, latency, bandwidth limits, and whether the server supports range requests.

That's why real-world testing matters more than marketing numbers.

3. What Happens When Your Internet Disconnects?

This is one of the biggest reasons I prefer using a dedicated download manager for large files.

Imagine:

File size: 60GB
Downloaded: 57GB
Progress: 95%

Then your Wi-Fi disconnects.

A good download manager should preserve the progress it has already made and continue when the connection comes back.

Instead of thinking:

"Start again."

The experience should be:

"Continue from where I stopped."

NeXDM is designed around resumable, segmented downloads so interrupted transfers can continue without unnecessarily downloading completed portions again.

4. Why NeXDM?

NeXDM is a Windows download manager built with a simple goal:

Make large downloads faster, lighter and easier to manage.

Its core features include:

⚡ Up to 64 download segments

🦀 Native Rust-based engine

🪶 Lightweight installation

🔄 Resume support

🌐 Browser integration

🧲 Native BitTorrent and magnet support

🛡️ No advertising

🔒 Privacy-focused design

🏪 Microsoft Store distribution

The idea isn't to replace every download tool for every user.

It's to provide a modern option for people who regularly download large files.

5. Why Rust?

NeXDM uses Rust for its core engine.

For a network-intensive desktop application, Rust is an interesting choice because it provides:

  • Native performance
  • Memory safety
  • Strong concurrency support
  • Low-level system control
  • No large managed runtime requirement

The result is a download manager designed to remain lightweight while handling multiple download streams.

For software that may sit in the background for hours, resource usage matters.

6. Direct Downloads + BitTorrent

Another useful feature is having different download workflows in one application.

Instead of using:

Browser
   +
Download Manager
   +
Torrent Client

NeXDM combines direct downloading with native BitTorrent/magnet support.

That means fewer applications to install and manage.

Of course, BitTorrent should only be used for content you have the legal right to download and share.

7. Browser Integration

Most downloads start in a browser.

You find a file.

You click Download.

That's it.

NeXDM is designed to integrate with Chromium-based browsers so users don't have to manually copy every download URL into a separate application.

The goal is simple:

Click Download
      ↓
NeXDM detects it
      ↓
Download is managed
      ↓
Pause / Resume / Continue
      ↓
File completed

The download manager should feel like part of the workflow—not another complicated tool you have to fight with.

8. What About Download Speed?

This is where it's important to be realistic.

A download manager cannot magically turn a 100 Mbps internet connection into 1 Gbps.

It also cannot guarantee maximum speed from every server.

Your actual speed can be limited by:

  • ISP bandwidth
  • Server bandwidth
  • Server-side throttling
  • Geographic distance
  • Network congestion
  • HTTP range support
  • Storage performance
  • Connection limits

But when the server and network support parallel downloads, segmented downloading can potentially make much better use of available bandwidth.

That's the real purpose of NeXDM's multi-segment engine.

9. Lightweight Software Matters

A download manager is usually a utility.

It shouldn't feel like a giant application suite.

You shouldn't need hundreds of megabytes of resources just to download a file.

NeXDM focuses on keeping the application lightweight while providing features normally associated with larger download managers.

That's especially useful for people who keep their download manager running in the background.

10. Who Should Use a Download Manager?

You probably don't need one if you're downloading a 2MB PDF once a week.

But a download manager becomes much more useful if you regularly download:

🎮 Large Games

Game installers and updates can easily reach tens of gigabytes.

🤖 AI Models

Models and datasets can be several gigabytes—or much larger.

🎬 Video Projects

High-resolution video files can consume hundreds of gigabytes.

💿 ISO Images

Developers and system administrators frequently download large operating-system images.

🧑‍💻 Developer Files

SDKs, archives, datasets and build artifacts can become large very quickly.

📦 Backups

Large backup archives benefit significantly from reliable resume support.

11. NeXDM vs. Using Only a Browser

The browser is excellent for everyday downloads.

But a dedicated download manager gives you more control.

Feature Browser NeXDM
Everyday downloads ✅ ✅
Large-file management Basic ✅
Segmented downloads Limited Up to 64 segments
Resume workflow Basic ✅
BitTorrent ❌ ✅
Magnet links ❌ ✅
Download queue/control Limited ✅
Dedicated download engine ❌ ✅

The browser isn't bad.

It's simply designed to do many things.

A download manager is designed specifically to manage downloads.

12. Is NeXDM Always Faster?

No—and that's important.

A good technical product should be honest about this.

If a server limits your connection to a certain speed, NeXDM cannot simply remove that limitation.

If your internet connection is slow, NeXDM cannot create bandwidth that doesn't exist.

If the server doesn't support the required range requests, segmented downloading may not provide the expected benefit.

But when conditions are favorable, parallel downloading can significantly improve throughput.

That's why the best way to evaluate NeXDM is simple:

Test it yourself.

Use the same file.

Use the same network.

Compare the results.

The Bigger Picture

The internet has changed.

Files are larger.

Internet connections are faster.

And users expect software to keep up.

A modern download manager should therefore focus on more than just "download faster."

It should provide:

Speed.

Reliability.

Resume support.

Low resource usage.

Privacy.

Simple browser integration.

Modern architecture.

That's the direction NeXDM is trying to take.

Final Thoughts

If you only download small files occasionally, your browser is probably enough.

But if you're regularly downloading 20GB, 50GB, 100GB+ files, a dedicated download manager can make the experience considerably easier.

NeXDM brings together segmented downloading, resumable transfers, browser integration, BitTorrent support and a lightweight Rust-based architecture in one Windows application.

It's not magic.

It can't change your ISP or the limitations of a remote server.

But it can give you a better tool for managing the bandwidth and connections you already have.

And in 2026, when a "large download" can mean 100GB or more, that's becoming increasingly important.

🚀 Try NeXDM

If you're interested in testing it yourself, check out the official website:

https://nexdm.in/

Run your own benchmark.

Compare it with your browser.

And see what difference a dedicated download engine makes on your connection.

What about you?

Do you still use your browser for 50GB+ downloads?

Or are you already using a dedicated download manager?

What's more important to you: speed, reliability, low RAM usage, privacy, or torrent support?

Let me know in the comments. 👇

#downloadmanager #windows #rust #opensource

title: 13 Attacks, 0 Vulnerabilities: Building a Security Toolkit With Zero Dependencies, ZeroVault
description:
TL;DR : I built a complete security toolkit (encrypted vault, TOTP authenticator, file encryptor, git secrets scanner, QR code generator, and a self-testing penetration suite) using nothing but Go's standard library. 82 files, 115 tests, 22 stdlib substitutions, zero packages. It then ran 13 automated attacks against itself and passed every one. Full source and demo at the bottom.

First, what's a "zero-dependency" project and why does anyone care?

Every time you run go get, npm install, or pip install, you're trusting someone else's code with your application. That sounds fine until you see the numbers:

  • 454,600 malicious packages were uploaded to registries last year alone
  • The average Node.js project has 683 transitive dependencies
  • One compromised package in your tree and your users' data is exposed

For security tools specifically, this is ironic. The software you trust to protect your passwords is itself trusting hundreds of packages you've never audited.

So a hackathon called Zero Dependency asked a simple, slightly rebellious question:

What if you built something genuinely useful using **nothing but the language itself?

No packages. No go get. Just Go's standard library. I said yes. Solo. Here's what happened.

What I built: ZeroVault, a security toolkit that ships as one binary

ZeroVault is everything you'd normally need three or four packages to build, packed into a single binary with an empty go.mod:

  • Encrypted password vault — AES-256-GCM encryption, PBKDF2 key derivation with 100,000 iterations
  • TOTP 2FA generator — RFC 6238 compatible, verified byte-for-byte against Google Authenticator
  • File encryption/decryption — streaming AES-GCM in 64KB chunks, handles files of any size
  • Secrets scanner — regex pattern matching + Shannon entropy analysis, scans current files AND git commit history by reading .git/objects directly
  • Password health dashboard — strength scoring, reuse detection, offline breach checking against 500 known compromised passwords
  • QR code generation — implemented from the ISO 18004 specification, Reed-Solomon and all
  • Vault 2FA — the vault protects itself using its own TOTP implementation
  • Clipboard auto-clear — passwords vanish from clipboard after 10 seconds
  • Web dashboard — premium UI with CSRF protection, XSS prevention, security headers, rate limiting
  • Automated penetration test suite — 13 real attacks with HTML audit report export
  • One-command demo mode — zerovault demo sets up everything for judges to try in 10 seconds

How you'd normally build this: go get a crypto library, a TOTP package, a web framework, a CSRF middleware, a QR encoder, a git library. Six dependencies minimum, each with their own dependency trees.

How I built it: composed crypto/aes, crypto/cipher, crypto/hmac, net/http, html/template, compress/zlib, regexp, and math from Go's standard library.

The proof:

$ cat go.mod
module zerovault

go 1.27

$ go list -m all
zerovault

That's it. That's the entire supply chain. One line: my own code.

The fun part: what I'd normally install, and what replaced it

This is the heart of the story. For each thing I needed, here's the package I'd usually grab, and the standard-library feature I used instead.

1. truffleHog → reading git's internals with compress/zlib

Normally I'd install: trufflesecurity/trufflehog (scans git history for leaked secrets)

What it actually takes: Git objects are just zlib-compressed files sitting in .git/objects/. The format is documented and surprisingly simple:

  • A commit object contains a tree hash, parent hash, author, and message
  • A tree object contains file entries: mode, name, and blob hash
  • A blob is the raw file content

I read them with compress/zlib, parsed the internal format with bytes and encoding/hex, and walked the commit graph backwards through parent hashes. When the scanner finds an AWS key in a blob that was deleted three commits ago, it reports: "deleted but still in history."

That's the exact feature people install truffleHog for. It took about 200 lines of stdlib Go. No git binary needed, no shelling out, no library. Just compress/zlib and string parsing.

The moment this worked, scanning a test repo and finding a Stripe key that had been "deleted" two commits prior — was probably the most satisfying moment of the entire hackathon.

2. pquerna/otp → TOTP in ~15 lines of HMAC

Normally I'd install: pquerna/otp or xlzd/gotp (TOTP/HOTP generation)

What it actually takes: Read RFC 6238. The entire TOTP algorithm is:

1. T = floor(unix_time / 30)
2. T_bytes = T as 8-byte big-endian
3. mac = HMAC-SHA1(secret, T_bytes)
4. offset = mac[19] & 0x0F
5. code = (mac[offset:offset+4] as uint32) & 0x7FFFFFFF
6. code = code % 1,000,000
7. Zero-pad to 6 digits

Go's stdlib has crypto/hmac, crypto/sha1, encoding/binary, and encoding/base32. Compose them exactly as the RFC says. The output matches Google Authenticator.

But here's where it gets meta: after building TOTP, I used it to protect the vault itself. zerovault 2fa enable generates a TOTP secret for the vault, and now unlocking requires both a master password AND a 6-digit code from your phone. I didn't install a 2FA library for the vault, I reused the TOTP code I'd already written.

Eating your own cooking. Zero additional lines of crypto.

3. gorilla/csrf → one line of stdlib

Normally I'd install: gorilla/csrf (CSRF protection middleware)

What it actually takes: Go 1.25 added CrossOriginProtection directly to net/http. It blocks cross-origin POST requests by checking the Origin header, the same approach gorilla/csrf uses internally.

One line to enable it. CSRF handled.

Combined with html/template (which auto-escapes dynamic content against XSS by default) and manually setting security headers (X-Frame-Options, CSP, no-cache), the entire web security layer came from stdlib. No middleware packages.

I verified this with automated tests: a curl POST with Origin: http://evil-site.com gets 403'd. The same request from localhost:8080 succeeds. The XSS tests inject <script>alert('hacked')</script> as a username, it renders as literal text in the browser. 8 different XSS payloads, all neutralized by html/template's auto-escaping.

4. QR code generation → math and patience

Normally I'd install: skip2/go-qrcode or any QR generation library

What it actually takes: This was the hardest single feature. QR codes involve:

  • Data encoding — numeric, alphanumeric, and byte modes with different bit lengths
  • Error correction — Reed-Solomon codes over GF(256), which means implementing Galois field arithmetic: addition (XOR), multiplication (log/antilog tables), polynomial division
  • Module placement — a specific pattern of data, error correction, format info, timing patterns, and alignment patterns
  • Masking — 8 different mask patterns, each scored for readability, pick the best one

I implemented all of it from the ISO/IEC 18004 specification. The GF(256) math alone — building the log/antilog lookup tables, computing generator polynomials, dividing data polynomials by generator polynomials — took real effort.

But when I ran zerovault totp qr github-2fa and Google Authenticator on my phone actually scanned the terminal output and added the account correctly, that was the single best moment of the hackathon.

No image library. No QR library. Just math, fmt, and stubbornness.

5. Password managers & breach databases → crypto/sha256 + embedded hashes

Normally I'd install: Something like a haveibeenpwned client or a breach database package

What it actually takes: I embedded the SHA-256 hashes of 500 commonly breached passwords directly in the source code. Not the passwords themselves, just their hashes. On every health check, each stored password is hashed and compared against the set.

"password123" → SHA-256 → check against embedded set → 
MATCH → "⚠ appears in breach databases"

Completely offline. No API calls. No internet. No dependency. The health dashboard shows a breach warning as a red banner that's impossible to miss.

The bug that almost killed my demo

During a hardening pass near the end, I ran go build -race and the race detector found something real.

The problem: Two concurrent HTTP requests could trigger simultaneous vault saves. On Windows, os.Rename (used for atomic file writes, write to temp file, rename over the original) doesn't behave atomically when the target file is open by another goroutine. The race detector caught it under a 60-request stress test.

How I found it: I almost didn't. The race only surfaces under concurrent web requests, my manual testing was always single-user. If I hadn't run the race detector as part of a systematic hardening pass, this would have surfaced live during the demo as a crash.

The fix: A per-session mutex held for the duration of each handler, plus unique temporary filenames per write operation (using a counter instead of a fixed name). The race detector confirmed the fix was clean.

The lesson: go build -race is not optional for concurrent Go code. This is the kind of bug a team of four catches in code review. Solo, the tooling has to catch it for you.

The attack suite: a security tool that tests itself

This is the feature I'm most proud of, and the one no other hackathon team built.

zerovault attack runs 13 automated penetration tests against the running application:

Crypto attacks:

  • Dictionary brute force — tries 20 common passwords, each takes ~0.3 seconds (PBKDF2 doing its job)
  • Vault bit-flip tampering — flips bits at 5 positions, GCM catches every one
  • Vault truncation/injection — tries appending, truncating, stripping the auth tag
  • PBKDF2 timing analysis — verifies no timing side-channel across password lengths
  • Nonce reuse detection — saves the vault 100 times, verifies all nonces are unique

Web attacks:

  • XSS injection — 8 different payloads (script tags, img onerror, SVG, template injection)
  • CSRF — 5 fake origins including null and wrong-port
  • Session security — no-cookie access, fake cookies, expired sessions, post-lock reuse
  • Security headers — verifies X-Frame-Options, CSP, nosniff, no-cache
  • Path traversal — tries ../../../etc/passwd and system directories on the scanner

TOTP attacks:

  • Code brute force — documents that TOTP security comes from the secret, not the code

The output is a terminal scoreboard AND a self-contained HTML audit report:

RESULTS: 10 blocked | 2 secure | 1 expected | 0 vulnerabilities

The attack scripts themselves are real code, attacks/bruteforce.go contains actual PBKDF2 derivation loops, attacks/xss.go sends real HTTP requests with real payloads and checks the response HTML for unescaped tags. I showed the source code in the demo video before running the suite so judges could see it wasn't fake output.

What the stdlib made painful

No argon2, no bcrypt, no scrypt

All three live in golang.org/x/crypto. Not stdlib. Can't use them.

PBKDF2 with 100,000 iterations is the OWASP minimum, and it's what I used. Is it as good as argon2? No, argon2 is memory-hard, which resists GPU attacks better. I documented this in the threat model:

"PBKDF2 is less resistant to GPU brute force than argon2. We chose PBKDF2 because argon2 requires golang.org/x/crypto, which is not part of Go's standard library."

Judges want honesty about tradeoffs, not false claims of invincibility.

Cross-platform password input without echo

golang.org/x/term is the clean way to read passwords without showing characters on screen. It's not stdlib. I used syscall directly, which works but requires different code paths for Unix and Windows. Annoying, but functional.

PBKDF2 itself

Go has crypto/hmac and crypto/sha256. It does NOT have a PBKDF2 function. I implemented it by composing HMAC in a loop per RFC 2898.

The implementation is maybe 40 lines. But those 40 lines are the foundation of the entire vault, if the key derivation is wrong, every encryption is wrong. I validated against RFC 6070 test vectors before writing anything else. Those test vectors were my first commit's first test.

What I didn't expect

  1. Go's stdlib is massive for security work. crypto/aes, crypto/cipher, crypto/hmac, crypto/sha256, crypto/rand, crypto/subtle, the entire AES-GCM + PBKDF2 + TOTP stack is in the box. I expected to hit walls. I didn't.

  2. TOTP is deceptively simple. The RFC looks intimidating. The implementation is HMAC + a counter + truncation. The perceived complexity around 2FA evaporates when you read the spec.

  3. Git's internal format is elegantly minimal. Zlib-compressed objects with a text header. No magic. Parse commits, follow trees, read blobs. A git history scanner doesn't need a git library, it needs compress/zlib and 200 lines of code.

  4. html/template is more sophisticated than most third-party alternatives. It doesn't just escape HTML, it escapes based on context (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, CSS, URL). Most template engines people install as dependencies don't do context-aware escaping this well.

  5. The constraint clarifies more than it limits. Every time I reached for a package, the stdlib already had the primitive. The missing piece was never the tool, it was knowing how to compose what was already there.

📊 ZeroVault by the Numbers 

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                                      │
│   ⏱  Build time ..................... ~12 hours     │
│                                                      │
│   📁 Go source files ................ 82            │
│                                                      │
│   ✅ Tests ........................... 115 (100%)   │
│                                                      │
│   📝 STDLIB.md entries .............. 22            │
│                                                      │
│   📦 Dependencies ................... 0             │
│                                                      │
│   🔒 Attack suite tests ............ 13             │
│                                                      │
│   🛡  Vulnerabilities found ......... 0              │ 
│                                                      │
│   🔄 Reproducible build ............ ✓ verified     │
│                                                      │
│   ⚡ AES-GCM throughput ............ ~1.0–1.6 GB/s   │
│                                                      │
│   🔑 PBKDF2 per attempt ............ ~300ms          │
│                                                      │
│   👤 Team size ...................... 1              │
│                                                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

What I'd change for production

Being honest:

  • Argon2 instead of PBKDF2 for memory-hard key derivation
  • TLS for the web dashboard (currently localhost HTTP only)
  • Secure memory wiping with mlock/munlock
  • OS keychain integration instead of clipboard
  • Hardware security key support (FIDO2/WebAuthn)
  • Audit log with cryptographic chaining for tamper detection

Every one of these requires dependencies outside Go's stdlib. That's the tradeoff, and articulating it honestly is what the hackathon is about.

The point

The zero-dependency constraint isn't about proving packages are bad. I'd use gorilla/csrf and truffleHog in production without hesitation.

The constraint is about understanding what sits underneath. When you install a TOTP library, do you know it's just HMAC-SHA1 with a time counter? When you use AES-GCM, do you know why GCM and not CBC? When you install a git scanning tool, do you know it's reading zlib-compressed objects from .git/objects/?

After this hackathon, I do. And that understanding doesn't go away when I go back to installing packages on Monday.

One binary. One person. Zero dependencies.

🔗 GitHub: github.com/Aaditya2010-14/zerovault

🎥 Demo video: YouTube Demo Video

Try it yourself:

git clone https://github.com/Aaditya2010-14/zerovault.git
cd zerovault
go build -o zerovault ./cmd/zerovault
./zerovault demo    # password: demo2026

Built for Zero Dependency Hackathon 2026 — Track E: Security & Crypto Utilities
